contraindications: Sorafenib in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis: not recommended (limited data, poor tolerance and survival)
interactions: Sorafenib with hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia: sorafenib prolongs the QT interval; correct potassium and magnesium and check an ECG before any further dose
Spironolactone with IV potassium replacement and reduced renal function: risk of rebound hyperkalemia; monitor potassium closely

Omeprazole: long-term proton pump inhibitor use causes hypomagnesemia and is associated with Clostridioides difficile infection and with hepatic encephalopathy and SBP in cirrhosis; no clinically relevant effect on sorafenib exposure
Lactulose and rifaximin: no clinically relevant interaction with sorafenib
output.proposed: Sorafenib 400 mg twice daily in cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy, diarrhea, potassium 2.8 mEq/L, magnesium 1.5 mg/dL and creatinine 1.5 mg/dL; with spironolactone, omeprazole, lactulose and rifaximin; IV potassium and magnesium proposed
warnings: Sorafenib diarrhea: interrupt treatment for grade 3 diarrhea or for grade 2 diarrhea with dehydration or electrolyte disturbance; resume at a reduced dose once resolved
Loperamide: antidiarrheal use counteracts lactulose and can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy; avoid while lactulose is being titrated
Avoid sedative drugs (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines) in hepatic encephalopathy

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.
Do not give loperamide while lactulose is treating HE; manage the diarrhea by holding sorafenib.
Do not resume sorafenib at full dose while diarrhea, hypokalemia and AKI persist.
required_recommendations: Identify and treat the precipitant: sorafenib-induced diarrhea with hypokalemia (K 2.8), hypomagnesemia (Mg 1.5) and pre-renal AKI (creatinine 1.5), and the fever.

Replace potassium to 4.0 mmol/L or more and replace magnesium, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis and hypomagnesemia impedes potassium repletion; monitor the ECG during IV potassium and hold spironolactone while creatinine is raised.
Treat the pre-renal AKI: stop spironolactone, replace the diarrheal volume losses, and give albumin 1 g/kg if creatinine does not improve after diuretic withdrawal (EASL 2018).
Fever without a source on the cultures, urinalysis, chest radiograph and stool C. difficile testing: re-examine for a source, and start empirical antibiotics if the fever persists without one.
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.

Continue lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); with 3-5 watery stools a day already, do not give loading doses, and adjust as the diarrhea settles; avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury. Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily.
Hold sorafenib until the diarrhea settles, then decide with oncology whether to resume it at a reduced dose; avoid loperamide while lactulose treats HE.
Oncology review of the HCC: AFP has risen from 1620 to 2840 ng/mL in three months; restage, and weigh further systemic therapy against Child-Pugh C liver function.
Stop omeprazole unless there is a specific indication: proton pump inhibitors are associated with HE, SBP, hypomagnesemia and C. difficile infection in cirrhosis (EASL 2022).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), alcoholic cirrhosis with HCC on sorafenib (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 25), precipitated by sorafenib-induced diarrhea causing hypokalemia (K 2.8), hypomagnesemia, dehydration and pre-renal AKI; concurrent fever with SBP excluded (ascitic PMN 188).

differential.key_features: Fever 38.2 °C with ascites, but ascitic PMN 188 cells/mm3, below 250, Gram stain and culture negative.
Fever and CRP 38 mg/L; blood and urine cultures, urinalysis, chest radiograph and stool C. difficile testing negative; no hypotension or raised lactate; asterixis favours HE.
Rare; PRES usually comes with severe hypertension, headache or visual symptoms; BP 126/76.
HCC rarely metastasises to the brain; no focal deficit; non-contrast CT shows no mass.
AKI follows diarrheal volume loss; reassess after diuretic withdrawal and volume replacement.
Dehydration is a precipitant here, not the sole cause, given cirrhosis with asterixis.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status; disorientation to time and place with somnolence (E3) is grade III.

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh C (14: bilirubin 4.2 3, albumin 2.3 3, INR 1.9 2, moderate ascites 3, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 25 (creatinine 1.5, bilirubin 4.2, INR 1.9, sodium 133)

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedatives, dehydration, renal failure.
Targeted therapies (sorafenib) commonly cause diarrhea; the electrolyte and volume consequences are a frequent HE precipitant in HCC patients on these drugs.
Fever in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites needs a diagnostic paracentesis; a PMN count below 250 cells/mm3 excludes SBP and the search for another source continues.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The sorafenib-related problem here is diarrhea with electrolyte and volume loss precipitating HE; direct CNS toxicity is rare.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute encephalopathy to HCC progression or 'sorafenib brain toxicity' and order extensive oncologic imaging.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fever with ascites needs paracentesis (PMN 188 excludes SBP), cultures, urinalysis, a chest radiograph and stool C. difficile testing (all negative here); start empirical antibiotics if the fever persists without a source.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the fever to the HCC or to sorafenib and skip the infection work-up.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T. is a 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma receiving sorafenib, presenting with a 1-week history of progressive confusion, word-finding difficulty, and behavioral change. His wife described increasing irritability, repeated conversations, and inability to balance his finances — activities he normally handles. He denies hematemesis or melena. He reports worsening nausea and diarrhea over the prior 3 weeks that his oncologist attributed to sorafenib side effects (sorafenib commonly causes diarrhea and nausea). His sorafenib dose has not been adjusted despite the diarrhea, which has been 3-5 watery stools per day. He has low-grade fever 38.2°C on admission.
